--- title: "Graph Metrics" subtitle: "The Basics of Social Network Analysis" format: revealjs: scrollable: true theme: default css: ucla-theme.css width: 1280 height: 720 margin: 0.1 min-scale: 0.2 --- # Node Neighborhoods --- ## Node Neighborhoods ::: {.incremental} - **Neighborhood** ($\mathcal{N}(v)$): - The set of nodes that are directly connected (adjacent) to node $v$. - These are a node's immediate **neighbors**. - Isolates have an empty neighborhood set ($\emptyset$). ::: --- ## Node Neighborhoods: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the graph on the right: - **Focal Node**: **4** (in tomato) - **Neighborhood**: $\mathcal{N}(4) = \{3, 7\}$ (in gold) - Another example: - $\mathcal{N}(1) = \{3\}$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-node-neighborhood-intro-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Neighborhood Intersection :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Neighborhood Intersection** ($\mathcal{N}(u) \cap \mathcal{N}(v)$) is the set of **common neighbors** connected to both $u$ and $v$. - In our graph: - $N(1) = \{3\}$ - $N(4) = \{3, 7\}$ - The intersection is the single node they share: - $N(1) \cap N(4) = \{3\}$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-neighborhood-intersection-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Neighborhood Intersection: Example 2 ::: {.incremental} - Let's find the neighborhood intersection of nodes **5** and **3**. - First, list their individual neighborhood sets: - $\mathcal{N}(5) = \{2, 6\}$ - $\mathcal{N}(3) = \{1, 2, 4\}$ - The intersection is the set of common neighbors they share: - $\mathcal{N}(5) \cap \mathcal{N}(3) = \{2\}$ ::: --- ## Neighborhood Intersection: Example 2 (Graph) :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Nodes **5** and **3** (in tomato) are not directly connected. - However, they share a common neighbor: node **2** (in gold). - Therefore, their neighborhood intersection is: $$\mathcal{N}(5) \cap \mathcal{N}(3) = \{2\}$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-neighborhood-intersection-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Neighborhood Union :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Neighborhood Union** ($\mathcal{N}(u) \cup \mathcal{N}(v)$) is the set of all nodes connected to *either* $u$ or $v$. - In our graph: - $N(1) = \{3\}$ - $N(4) = \{3, 7\}$ - The union contains all unique neighbors from both sets: - $N(1) \cup N(4) = \{3, 7\}$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-neighborhood-union-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Neighborhood Union: Example 2 ::: {.incremental} - Let's find the neighborhood union of nodes **5** and **3**. - First, list their individual neighborhood sets: - $\mathcal{N}(5) = \{2, 6\}$ - $\mathcal{N}(3) = \{1, 2, 4\}$ - The union combines all unique neighbors from both sets: - $\mathcal{N}(5) \cup \mathcal{N}(3) = \{1, 2, 4, 6\}$ ::: --- ## Neighborhood Union: Example 2 (Graph) :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Focal nodes **5** and **3** are shown in tomato. - The union of their neighbors (nodes **1, 2, 4, 6**) is shown in gold. - Therefore, the union of neighbors is: $$\mathcal{N}(5) \cup \mathcal{N}(3) = \{1, 2, 4, 6\}$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-neighborhood-union-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- # Directed Graph Elements & Metrics --- ## Asymmetric Ties & Directed Graphs ::: {.incremental} - Some relationships have an inherent **directionality** (**asymmetric ties**): - e.g., "A helps B", "A seeks advice from B". - Unlike symmetric ties, **mutuality** or **reciprocity** is not guaranteed by definition. - Reciprocity is an empirical event in the world (mutuality must be measured rather than assumed). ::: --- ## Anti-Symmetric Ties & Hierarchies ::: {.incremental} - Some directional relationships strictly forbid reciprocity (**anti-symmetric ties**): - If $A \rightarrow B$ exists, then $B \rightarrow A$ is structurally or logically impossible ($AB \implies \neg BA$). - e.g., "A is the father of B", "A is the supervisor of B". - Unlike asymmetric ties, reciprocity is not optional—it is strictly prohibited. - Concatenating these relations across multiple nodes naturally generates **directed trees** or **strict hierarchies** with no cycles. ::: --- ## Directed Graph Representation ::: {.incremental} - Asymmetric networks are represented as a **directed graph** (or **digraph**): - Simple lines are replaced with **arrows** indicating directionality. - Every edge has a **source node** (sender) and a **destination node** (receiver). - Unlike undirected graphs, node order matters: edge $AB$ is distinct from $BA$. ::: --- ## Directed Graph: An Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the digraph on the right: - Arrows indicate the direction of the relationship. - Some ties are **reciprocated** (e.g., $A \leftrightarrow B$ and $B \leftrightarrow D$). - Others are strictly **asymmetric** (e.g., $E \rightarrow C$, $G \rightarrow F$). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-dir-intro-graph-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Neighborhoods in Directed Graphs (1) :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Because links are directional, nodes have two neighborhoods. - **In-Neighborhood** ($N^{in}(v)$): - Set of source nodes pointing *to* $v$. - Example: $N^{in}(D) = \{B, E, G\}$ (highlighted in gold, pointing to focal node D in tomato). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Neighborhoods in Directed Graphs (2) :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Out-Neighborhood** ($N^{out}(v)$): - Set of destination nodes that $v$ points *to*. - Example: $N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}$ (highlighted in gold, pointing from focal node B in tomato). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Neighborhoods: Reciprocity :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - A node appears in both neighborhoods only if there is a **reciprocal** (mutual) tie. - Example for Node **B** (in tomato): - In-Neighborhood: $N^{in}(B) = \{A\}$ - Out-Neighborhood: $N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Neighborhoods: Reciprocity Overlap :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Since there is a reciprocal tie $A \leftrightarrow B$, node **A** (in gold) belongs to both sets. - Therefore, the overlap is the intersection of these two neighborhoods: $$N^{in}(B) \cap N^{out}(B) = \{A\}$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Neighborhood Intersection ::: {.incremental} - In directed graphs, neighborhood intersections can be defined for incoming or outgoing ties: - **In-Neighborhood Intersection**: Common source nodes pointing to both $u$ and $v$: - $N^{in}(D) \cap N^{in}(A) = \{B\}$ (Node $B$ points to both $D$ and $A$) - **Out-Neighborhood Intersection**: Common destination nodes that both $u$ and $v$ point to: - $N^{out}(B) \cap N^{out}(E) = \{D\}$ (Both $B$ and $E$ point to $D$) ::: --- ## Directed Neighborhood Intersection: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's visualize the **out-neighborhood intersection** of nodes **B** and **E** (in tomato): - $N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}$ - $N^{out}(E) = \{D\}$ - They share one common destination node: - $N^{out}(B) \cap N^{out}(E) = \{D\}$ (in gold) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Neighborhood Union ::: {.incremental} - Similarly, directed neighborhood unions combine the sets of neighbors: - **In-Neighborhood Union**: Nodes pointing to either $u$ or $v$: - $N^{in}(D) \cup N^{in}(A) = \{B, E, G\}$ - **Out-Neighborhood Union**: Nodes that either $u$ or $v$ points to: - $N^{out}(B) \cup N^{out}(E) = \{A, C, D\}$ ::: --- ## Directed Neighborhood Union: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's visualize the **out-neighborhood union** of nodes **B** and **E** (in tomato): - $N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}$ - $N^{out}(E) = \{D\}$ - Combining all unique destination nodes gives: - $N^{out}(B) \cup N^{out}(E) = \{A, C, D\}$ (in gold) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: # Special Classes of Directed Graphs --- ## Symmetric Directed Graphs :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Symmetric Directed Graph**: - A digraph where for every directed arc $u \rightarrow v$, the reverse arc $v \rightarrow u$ is also present. - Formally: $AB \iff BA$. - **Key Properties**: - It is a directed representation of an undirected (symmetric) graph. - Every connected dyad is **reciprocal** (Mutual). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Functional Graphs :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Functional Graph**: - A directed graph where every node has an outdegree of **exactly 1**: $$k^{out}_v = 1 \quad \text{for all } v \in V$$ - **Key Properties**: - Represents a single-valued function $f: V \rightarrow V$, mapping each node to exactly one target. - e.g., "Who is your best friend?" or "Who is your immediate boss?" ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Oriented Graphs :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Oriented Graph**: - A directed graph obtained by choosing a **single direction** for each edge in an undirected graph. - **Key Properties**: - **No reciprocal (mutual) arcs** can exist: if $u \rightarrow v$ is present, then $v \rightarrow u$ is forbidden. - Represents purely non-reciprocal systems of interaction or asymmetric flows. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Tree Graphs :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Directed Tree Graph**: - A directed, acyclic graph where a single root node has an indegree of 0, and all other nodes have an indegree of **exactly 1**: $$k^{in}_{root} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad k^{in}_v = 1 \quad \text{for all other } v$$ - **Key Properties**: - Naturally models **strict authority hierarchies** or family trees. - Every node has exactly one parent or supervisor, with zero loops or overlapping chains of command. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- # Node Degree --- ## Node Degree in Undirected Graphs ::: {.incremental} - In an undirected graph, a node's **degree** ($k_i$) has two equivalent definitions: 1. **Neighborhood Cardinality**: The number of neighbors of node $i$ ($k_i = |\mathcal{N}(i)|$). 2. **Incident Edges Count**: The number of edges connected to node $i$. - Sociological meaning: **Degree Centrality** (reflects popularity, influence, or activity). ::: --- ## Node Degree: An Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's calculate the degree for Node **A** (in tomato) on the right: - Neighbors of **A**: $\mathcal{N}(A) = \{B, C, D, F\}$ - Neighborhood size: $k_A = |\mathcal{N}(A)| = 4$ - Incident edges: $AB$, $AC$, $AD$, and $AF$ ($k_A = 4$) - Thus, the degree of Node **A** is **4**. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Endpoints in Undirected Graphs ::: {.incremental} - **Endpoints** (or leaves/periphery): - Nodes that have a degree equal to **one** ($k_i = 1$). - They have just a single neighbor in the graph. ::: --- ## Endpoints: An Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's identify the endpoints in the graph on the right: - Nodes **C** and **F** (in tomato) are connected only to node **A**. - Since $k_C = 1$ and $k_F = 1$, they have degree one. - Therefore, **C** and **F** are the endpoints of this graph. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Node Degree in Directed Graphs: Indegree ::: {.incremental} - Directed graphs have two distinct degrees for each node. - **Indegree** ($k^{in}_i$): - Number of edges pointing to node $i$ (cardinality of $N^{in}(i)$). - Sociological meaning: **Popularity, Prestige, or Status**. ::: --- ## Indegree: An Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's find the indegree for Node **D** (in tomato) on the right: - Source nodes pointing to **D**: $N^{in}(D) = \{B, E, G\}$ (in gold) - Indegree: $k^{in}_D = |N^{in}(D)| = 3$ - Node **D** has 3 incoming arrows, representing a node with relatively high popularity or status. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Node Degree in Directed Graphs: Outdegree ::: {.incremental} - **Outdegree** ($k^{out}_i$): - Number of edges pointing from node $i$ (cardinality of $N^{out}(i)$). - Sociological meaning: **Sociability or Activity**. ::: --- ## Outdegree: An Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's find the outdegree for Node **B** (in tomato) on the right: - Target nodes that **B** points to: $N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}$ (in gold) - Outdegree: $k^{out}_B = |N^{out}(B)| = 3$ - Node **B** has 3 outgoing arrows, representing a node with relatively high sociability or activity. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- --- ## Types of Nodes in Directed Graphs ::: {.incremental} - In a directed graph, we can distinguish three types of (non-isolate) nodes based on incoming and outgoing ties: 1. **Receivers**: Nodes that receive ties but do not send them ($k_{in} > 0$ and $k_{out} = 0$). 2. **Transmitters**: Nodes that send ties but do not receive them ($k_{in} = 0$ and $k_{out} > 0$). 3. **Carriers**: Nodes that both receive and send ties ($k_{in} > 0$ and $k_{out} > 0$). ::: --- ## Node Types: An Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Looking at the directed graph on the right: - **Receiver**: Node **C** (only receives ties). - **Transmitters**: Nodes **E** and **G** (only send ties). - **Carriers**: Nodes **A**, **B**, **D**, **F** (both receive and send ties). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/plt-dir-node-types-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- # Basic Graph Metrics --- ## Graph Order and Size ::: {.incremental} - **Graph Order** ($n$): - The number of nodes in the graph ($n = |V|$). - Cardinality of the vertex set. - **Graph Size** ($m$): - The number of edges in the graph ($m = |E|$). - Cardinality of the edge set. ::: --- ## Order and Size: Undirected Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the undirected graph on the right: - **Node Set** ($V$): $\{A, B, C, D, E, F, G\}$ - **Edge Set** ($E$): $\{AC, CD, DG,$
$BE, EF, FB, CB\}$ - **Graph Order** ($n = |V|$): **7** nodes - **Graph Size** ($m = |E|$): **7** edges ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Order and Size: Directed Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the directed graph on the right: - **Node Set** ($V$): $\{A, B, C, D, E, G\}$ - **Edge Set** ($E$): $\{BA, BC, BD, ED,$
$GD, AE, CG, AB\}$ - **Graph Order** ($n = |V|$): **6** nodes - **Graph Size** ($m = |E|$): **8** edges ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Graph Maximum Size ::: {.incremental} - The **maximum size** of a simple graph of order $n$ is the number of edges in a **complete graph** (where every node is connected to every other node). - Undirected: $Max(E) = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}$ - Directed: $Max(E) = n(n - 1)$ ::: --- ## Maximum Size: Undirected Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the undirected graph on the right: - **Order** ($n$): 7 nodes - **Formula**: $$Max(E) = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Maximum Size: Undirected Calculation :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Order** ($n$): 7 nodes (shown on the right) - **Maximum possible size** calculation: $$Max(E) = \frac{7 \times (7 - 1)}{2} = \frac{42}{2} = 21\text{ edges}$$ - **Interpretation**: - A complete undirected graph with 7 nodes would have exactly **21** edges. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Maximum Size: Directed Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the directed graph on the right: - **Order** ($n$): 6 nodes - **Formula**: $$Max(E) = n(n - 1)$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Maximum Size: Directed Calculation :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Order** ($n$): 6 nodes (shown on the right) - **Maximum possible size** calculation: $$Max(E) = 6 \times (6 - 1) = 6 \times 5 = 30\text{ edges}$$ - **Interpretation**: - A complete directed graph with 6 nodes would have exactly **30** directed arcs. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Graph Density: Formulas ::: {.incremental} - **Density** ($d$) is the ratio of the observed number of edges ($m$) to the maximum possible number of edges. - It is a value between 0 (completely empty) and 1 (complete graph). - **Undirected Graph**: $$d = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}$$ ::: --- --- ## Graph Density: Formulas ::: {.incremental} - **Density** ($d$) is the ratio of the observed number of edges ($m$) to the maximum possible number of edges. - It is a value between 0 (completely empty) and 1 (complete graph). - **Directed Graph**: $$d = \frac{m}{n(n-1)}$$ ::: --- ## Graph Density: Interpretation ::: {.incremental} - **Connection Probability**: - Density is the probability that any two randomly chosen nodes are connected. - **Network Resilience**: - Denser networks are generally more resilient and less vulnerable to breakdowns when key nodes are removed. ::: --- ## Density: Undirected Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the undirected graph on the right: - **Order** ($n$): 7 nodes - **Size** ($m$): 7 edges - **Maximum possible edges**: $$Max(E) = \frac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Density: Undirected Calculation :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Observed edges** ($m$): 7 (shown on the right) - **Maximum possible edges**: 21 - **Density Formula**: $$d = \frac{m}{Max(E)} = \frac{7}{21} \approx 0.333$$ - **Interpretation**: - Exactly **33.3%** of all possible undirected ties are present in this network. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Density: Directed Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's look at the directed graph on the right: - **Order** ($n$): 6 nodes - **Size** ($m$): 8 directed edges - **Maximum possible edges**: $$Max(E) = 6 \times 5 = 30$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Density: Directed Calculation :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Observed directed edges** ($m$): 8 (shown on the right) - **Maximum possible edges**: 30 - **Density Formula**: $$d = \frac{m}{Max(E)} = \frac{8}{30} \approx 0.267$$ - **Interpretation**: - Exactly **26.7%** of all possible directed ties are present in this network. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- # Degree-Based Graph Metrics --- ## Graph Degree Set and Sequence :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Graph Degree Set**: A list of the degrees of every node in the graph. - **Graph Degree Sequence**: The degree set sorted in descending order. - This provides a "fingerprint" of the graph's overall connectivity structure. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Degree Set & Sequence: Undirected Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Degrees**: $k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **Degree Set** (unordered list of node degrees): $$\{1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1\}$$ - **Degree Sequence** (sorted degrees): $$(3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1)$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## In-Degree Set & Sequence: Directed Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **In-Degrees**: $k^{in}_A=1, k^{in}_B=1, k^{in}_C=1, k^{in}_D=3, k^{in}_E=1, k^{in}_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **In-Degree Set** (unordered list of in-degrees): $$\{1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1\}$$ - **In-Degree Sequence** (sorted in-degrees): $$(3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Out-Degree Set & Sequence: Directed Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Out-Degrees**: $k^{out}_A=2, k^{out}_B=3, k^{out}_C=1, k^{out}_D=0, k^{out}_E=1, k^{out}_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **Out-Degree Set** (unordered list of out-degrees): $$\{2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1\}$$ - **Out-Degree Sequence** (sorted out-degrees): $$(3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0)$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Degree Range & Sum :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Maximum Degree** ($k_{max}$) and **Minimum Degree** ($k_{min}$). - **Degree Range** ($k_r$): $k_{max} - k_{min}$. - **Sum of Degrees** ($\sum k_i$): - In an undirected graph, this is always twice the number of edges: $\sum k_i = 2m$. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Degree Range & Sum: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Degrees**: $k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **Max & Min Degree**: - $k_{max} = 3$ (nodes B and C) - $k_{min} = 1$ (nodes A and G) - **Degree Range**: - $k_r = 3 - 1 = 2$ - **Sum of Degrees**: - $\sum k_i = 1+3+3+2+2+2+1 = 14 = 2m$ (Matches!) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Graphical vs. Non-Graphical Sequences ::: {.incremental} - A sequence of non-negative integers is **graphical** if there exists at least one simple, undirected graph (no loops, no multiple edges) that has it as its degree sequence. - Otherwise, the sequence is **non-graphical**—no such simple graph can possibly exist in the real world. - Why can't certain sequences exist? - They violate core mathematical rules of graph structure! ::: --- ## Two Quick Tests for Graphicality Before using complex algorithms, we can apply two fast screening tests: ::: {.incremental} 1. **The Even Sum Rule (Handshake Lemma)**: - The sum of degrees must be **even**: $\sum k_i = 2m$. - *If the sum of a sequence is odd, it is automatically non-graphical!* 2. **The Maximum Degree Bound**: - In a simple graph of order $n$, no node can have a degree larger than $n-1$. - *If any degree in the sequence exceeds $n-1$, it is automatically non-graphical!* ::: --- ## Graphicality: Concrete Examples ::: {.incremental} - **Graphical Sequence**: $\mathbf{d} = (4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1)$ with $n = 7$ - Sum is $16$ (even). Max degree is $4 \le 6$. - A real simple graph can easily be constructed with these degrees. - **Non-Graphical Sequence (Odd Sum Violation)**: $\mathbf{d} = (4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 1)$ with $n = 7$ - Sum is $17$ (odd). Violates Handshake Lemma. - *No simple graph can ever have this sequence.* - **Non-Graphical Sequence (Degree Bound Violation)**: $\mathbf{d} = (7, 2, 2, 1)$ with $n = 4$ - Max degree is $7$, which is greater than $n-1 = 3$. - *A node in a 4-person group cannot have 7 unique friends!* ::: ## Average Degree :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Average Degree** ($\bar{k}$): The average of all node degrees in the graph. $$\bar{k} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} k_i = \frac{2m}{n}$$ - It represents the expected degree of a randomly chosen node. - It is also directly related to density, which we will derive on the next slides! ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Connecting Density & Average Degree ::: {.incremental} - There is an **intimate mathematical relationship** between density ($d$) and average degree ($\bar{k}$). - Recall the undirected density formula: $$d = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}$$ - We can rewrite this by pulling out the average degree term ($\bar{k} = \frac{2m}{n}$): $$d = \left(\frac{2m}{n}\right) \times \frac{1}{n-1} = \bar{k} \times \frac{1}{n-1} = \frac{\bar{k}}{n-1} \qquad \iff \qquad \bar{k} = d(n-1)$$ ::: --- ## Interpreting the Density-Degree Connection ::: {.incremental} - **Density is Average Degree Scaled by Group Size**: - The density of an undirected graph is simply its average degree divided by the maximum possible connections of any single node ($n-1$). - **For Example**: - In a group of $n = 10$ people, each person can have at most $n-1 = 9$ connections. - If the average number of friends ($\bar{k}$) is $4.5$, then the density of friendship is: $$d = \frac{4.5}{9} = 0.50 \quad (50\%)$$ - **Directed Case**: - The exact same identity holds! Since $d^d = \frac{m}{n(n-1)}$ and \bar{k} is $\frac{m}{n}$, we get: $$d^d = \frac{\bar{k}}{n-1}$$ ::: --- ## Degree Variance :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_k$): A measure of how much the node degrees vary from the average degree. $$\sigma^2_k = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (k_i - \bar{k})^2$$ - A low variance mean less inequality in connectivity (more homogeneous), while a high variance indicates more inequality (more heterogeneous). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Degree Metrics: Basic Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Node Degrees**: $k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **Degree Set**: $\{1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1\}$ (degrees of all nodes in the graph) - **Degree Sequence**: $(3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1)$ (ordered from highest to lowest) - **Degree Sum**: $$\sum k_i = 1+3+3+2+2+2+1 = 14 = 2m$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Degree Metrics: Average Degree :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Degrees**: $k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **Order** ($n$): 7 nodes - **Average Degree** ($\bar{k}$): $$\bar{k} = \frac{\sum k_i}{n} = \frac{14}{7} = 2.0$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Degree Metrics: Degree Variance :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Degrees**: $k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1$ (shown on the right) - **Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_k$): $$\sigma^2_k = \frac{\sum (k_i - \bar{k})^2}{n}$$ - **Variance Calculation**: $$\sigma^2_k = \frac{3 \times (2-2)^2 + 2 \times (3-2)^2 + 2 \times (1-2)^2}{7} = \frac{4}{7} \approx 0.571$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Regular Graphs :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - A **regular graph** is one where every node has the same degree $k$ (called **$k$-regular**). - Since all node degrees are identical to the average, the degree variance is zero ($\sigma^2_k = 0$). - These are rare in real-world social networks but are used as baseline models. - Example: A **3-regular** graph on 6 nodes (shown on the right). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){fig-align='center' width=432} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Regular Graphs: Metrics Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Node Degrees**: $k_A=3, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=3, k_E=3, k_F=3$ (shown on the right) - **Order** ($n$): 6 nodes - **Average Degree** ($\bar{k}$): $$\bar{k} = \frac{\sum k_i}{n} = \frac{18}{6} = 3.0$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){fig-align='center' width=432} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Regular Graphs: Variance Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Average Degree** ($\bar{k}$): 3.0 (shown on the right) - **Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_k$): $$\sigma^2_k = \frac{6 \times (3 - 3)^2}{6} = 0$$ - **Conclusion**: - Since every node's degree matches the average degree, the deviation is zero for all nodes, resulting in **zero variance**. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-38-1.png){fig-align='center' width=432} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Average Nearest Neighbor Degree :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Average Nearest Neighbor Degree** ($\bar{k}_{nn(i)}$) measures the average degree of node $i$'s neighbors. - Formula: $$\bar{k}_{nn(i)} = \frac{1}{k_i} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} k_j$$ - It tells us whether a node's connections are, on average, highly connected or peripheral. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Feld's Friendship Paradox ::: {.incremental} - **Feld's Friendship Paradox** (Scott Feld, 1991): - In almost all social networks, the average degree of a node's neighbors ($\bar{k}_{nn}$) is **greater** than the average degree of the nodes in the network ($\bar{k}$). - Why does this happen? - Highly connected individuals (popular hubs) belong to many people's neighborhood sets, disproportionately inflating neighbor degrees across the network. - **Your friends, on average, have more friends than you do!** ::: --- ## Friendship Paradox: Node Calculations (A-D) ::: {.incremental} - For the undirected graph shown previously (average degree $\bar{k} = 2.0$): - **Node A** (neighbor C): $\bar{k}_{nn(A)} = \frac{k_C}{1} = \frac{3}{1} = 3.0$ - **Node B** (neighbors C, E, F): $\bar{k}_{nn(B)} = \frac{k_C + k_E + k_F}{3} = \frac{3 + 2 + 2}{3} \approx 2.33$ - **Node C** (neighbors A, D, B): $\bar{k}_{nn(C)} = \frac{k_A + k_D + k_B}{3} = \frac{1 + 2 + 3}{3} = 2.0$ - **Node D** (neighbors C, G): $\bar{k}_{nn(D)} = \frac{k_C + k_G}{2} = \frac{3 + 1}{2} = 2.0$ ::: --- ## Friendship Paradox: Node Calculations (E-G) ::: {.incremental} - Continuing calculations for the remaining nodes: - **Node E** (neighbors B, F): $\bar{k}_{nn(E)} = \frac{k_B + k_F}{2} = \frac{3 + 2}{2} = 2.5$ - **Node F** (neighbors E, B): $\bar{k}_{nn(F)} = \frac{k_E + k_B}{2} = \frac{2 + 3}{2} = 2.5$ - **Node G** (neighbor D): $\bar{k}_{nn(G)} = \frac{k_D}{1} = \frac{2}{1} = 2.0$ - **Summary of average neighbor degrees**: - $\bar{k}_{nn} = (3.0, 2.33, 2.0, 2.0, 2.5, 2.5, 2.0)$ ::: --- ## Friendship Paradox: Network Average ::: {.incremental} - From the node calculations on the previous slide, the average nearest neighbor degrees are: - $\bar{k}_{nn} = (3.0, 2.33, 2.0, 2.0, 2.5, 2.5, 2.0)$ - **Average neighbor degree** for the network: $$\text{Mean}(\bar{k}_{nn}) = \frac{3.0 + 2.33 + 2.0 + 2.0 + 2.5 + 2.5 + 2.0}{7} \approx 2.33$$ - **Demonstrating the Paradox**: - Average degree of nodes' neighbors ($\approx 2.33$) is **greater** than the average degree of nodes ($\bar{k} = 2.0$). ::: --- # Directed Graph Elements & Metrics --- ## Directed Degree Sets & Sequences ::: {.incremental} - Directed graphs have two distinct degree sets (In-Degree set and Out-Degree set) and two distinct sequences. - In our 6-node directed graph: - **In-Degree Set**: $\{1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1\}$ - **In-Degree Sequence**: $(3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$ - **Out-Degree Set**: $\{2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1\}$ - **Out-Degree Sequence**: $(3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0)$ ::: --- ## Directed Degree Range & Sum ::: {.incremental} - Like undirected graphs, we can define the maximum, minimum, and range of degrees. - In directed graphs, these are defined separately for in-degree and out-degree: - **In-Degree Range**: $k^{in}_{max} - k^{in}_{min}$ - **Out-Degree Range**: $k^{out}_{max} - k^{out}_{min}$ - **Degree Sum Rule**: - The sum of in-degrees and the sum of out-degrees are both equal to the graph size $m$ (total number of directed edges/arcs): $\sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{in}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{out}_i = m$ ::: --- ## Directed Range & Sum: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.incremental} - For our 6-node directed graph (shown again on the right, $m = 8$): - **In-Degrees**: $k^{in} = (1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1)$ - $k^{in}_{max} = 3$ (Node D), $k^{in}_{min} = 1$ - Range $k^{in}_r = 3 - 1 = 2$ - Sum $\sum k^{in}_i = 1+1+1+3+1+1 = 8$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Range & Sum: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.incremental} - For our 6-node directed graph (shown again on the right, $m = 8$): - **Out-Degrees**: $k^{out} = (2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1)$ - $k^{out}_{max} = 3$ (Node B), $k^{out}_{min} = 0$ (Node D) - Range $k^{out}_r = 3 - 0 = 3$ - Sum $\sum k^{out}_i = 2+3+1+0+1+1 = 8$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-41-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Average Degree ::: {.incremental} - **Average In-Degree** ($\bar{k}^{in}$) and **Average Out-Degree** ($\bar{k}^{out}$): $\bar{k}^{in} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{in}_i \quad \text{and} \quad \bar{k}^{out} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{out}_i$ - **The Equivalence Theorem**: - In *every* directed graph, the average in-degree is **exactly equal** to the average out-degree: $\bar{k}^{in} = \bar{k}^{out} = \frac{m}{n}$ - **Why?** Each directed edge $u \rightarrow v$ adds exactly **1** to the out-degree of $u$ and exactly **1** to the in-degree of $v$. ::: --- ## Equivalence of Means: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.incremental} - In our 6-node directed graph: - **Order** ($n$): 6 nodes - **Size** ($m$): 8 directed edges - **Mean In-Degree**: $\bar{k}^{in} = \frac{1+1+1+3+1+1}{6} = \frac{8}{6} \approx 1.33$ - **Mean Out-Degree**: $\bar{k}^{out} = \frac{2+3+1+0+1+1}{6} = \frac{8}{6} \approx 1.33$ - **They are equal!** ($\bar{k}^{in} = \bar{k}^{out} = 1.33 = m/n$) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-42-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Degree Variance ::: {.incremental} - While the means are always equal, the **variances** of in-degree and out-degree can be completely different! - **In-Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_{in}$): $\sigma^2_{in} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (k^{in}_i - \bar{k}^{in})^2$ - Sociological meaning: Measures inequality in **prestige/popularity** (do a few nodes receive all ties?). - **Out-Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_{out}$): $\sigma^2_{out} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (k^{out}_i - \bar{k}^{out})^2$ - Sociological meaning: Measures inequality in **sociability/activity** (do some nodes send way more ties than others?). ::: --- ## Directed Degree Variance: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.incremental} - In our 6-node directed graph: - Mean degree ($\bar{k}$) is $\approx 1.33$ - **In-Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_{in}$): - Values: - $k^{in} = (1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1)$ - Calculation: - $\frac{5 \times (1-1.33)^2 + 1 \times (3-1.33)^2}{6} =$ - $\frac{5 \times 0.11 + 2.78}{6} \approx 0.556$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-43-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Directed Degree Variance: Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.incremental} - In our 6-node directed graph: - Mean degree ($\bar{k}$) is $\approx 1.33$ - **Out-Degree Variance** ($\sigma^2_{out}$): - Values: - $k^{out} = (2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1)$ - Calculation: - $\frac{(2-1.33)^2 + (3-1.33)^2 + 3(1-1.33)^2 + (0-1.33)^2}{6} \approx 0.889$ - Out-degree is **more heterogeneous** than in-degree in this network! ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](graph-metrics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-44-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Comparing Density: Undirected vs. Directed ::: {.incremental} - **Maximum Possible Edges**: - Undirected: $Max(E)_{undir} = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}$ - Directed: $Max(E)_{dir} = n(n - 1)$ - **Density Scaling**: - Because a directed graph can hold exactly twice as many edges as an undirected graph of the same order: $d_{dir} = \frac{1}{2} d_{undir} \quad \text{for the same } m \text{ and } n$ - Directed density is always more "conservative"—it requires twice as many edges as an undirected graph to reach the same level of density! ::: --- ## Density Scaling: A Direct Comparison | Metric | Undirected Graph | Directed Graph | |:-------|:----------------:|:--------------:| | **Formula** | $d = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}$ | $d = \frac{m}{n(n-1)}$ | | **Max Edges ($n = 6$)** | $15$ edges | $30$ edges | | **If $m = 8$ edges** | $d \approx 0.533 \quad (53.3\%)$ | $d \approx 0.267 \quad (26.7\%)$ | | **If $m = 15$ edges** | $d = 1.000 \quad (100.0\%)$ | $d = 0.500 \quad (50.0\%)$ | : Density Comparison Matrix {#tbl-density-scaling}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
